question:
Which of the below has not undergone trisyllabic laxing during its sound development: 

southern, derivative, serenity, pleasant, gratitude, shadow

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is shadow, because unlike the others (e.g. south → southern with the vowel shift, or serene → serenity), shadow derives from OE sceadu/sceadwe where the short vowel was already present in disyllabic forms and shows no evidence of the trisyllabic laxing process applying later in its development. The other words all have clear etymological alternations showing a long vowel reduced due to added syllables.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is shadow. Trisyllabic laxing is a historical shortening process that applies when a long vowel is followed by two additional syllables in the derived form, as seen in pairs like serene/serenity or divine/divinity. Southern shows the expected laxing from south (with its diphthong shortening to /ʌ/ in the trisyllabic southern), derivative and serenity clearly reflect it from their bases, pleasant from please, and gratitude from the Latin source with its short vowel in the three-syllable form. Shadow, however, is only disyllabic (from OE sceadu) and shows no evidence of that three-syllable conditioning in its development, so it seems to be the one that hasn't undergone the process.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Shadow is the clear non-member of the set and southern is the other disyllabic
Germanic item in the list.

Trisyllabic laxing is the early ModE shortening/laxation of a long stressed vowel
when the stressed syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables,
e.g. /iː/ > /ɪ/, /eː/ > /ɛ/, /aː/ > /æ/ etc. The process is essentially a Romance/
learned Latinate phenomenon. 

* derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/ < L. derivatīvus. The stressed /i/ of the stem,
cf. derive /dɪˈraɪv/ ~ /dɪˈriːv/  > /ɪ/ in the trisyllabic derivative.
* serenity /səˈrɛnəti/ < L. serenitas. Cf. serene /səˈriːn/. The stem vowel
/eː/  is laxed to /ɛ/ in the three- / four-syllable serenity.
* gratitude /ˈɡrætitjuːd/ < L. gratitudo. The initial stressed vowel of the
stem is the laxed reflex of an earlier long /aː/ in a trisyllabic environment,
cf. the same stem in the bisyllabic grant.

Pleasant < OFr. plaisant is a Romance loan and shows the same type of vowel
shortening that is normally described under trisyllabic laxing, and it is
routinely cited with derivative, serenity and gratitude as a Latinate
development.

Shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ < OE sceadu, PGmc *skadwō is a native Germanic disyllabic
word with an original short vowel. It has never had a three-syllable
stressed form with a long vowel to be laxed, and it is to this day
bi-syllabic. Southern /ˈsaʊðən/ < OE sūðerne is the other Germanic
disyllabic item in the list: it is always bi-syllabic and its diphthong /aʊ/
is the regular reflex of OE /uː/, not the product of trisyllabic laxing.
That is why shadow, and southern, are the odd men out vis-à-vis the
Latinate trisyllabically laxed set derivative-serenity-gratitude.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: southern

Trisyllabic shortening / trisyllabic laxing is the regular English
tendency for a long/stressed vowel to be shortened and laxed when the
stem is expanded to a word of three or more syllables with the stress
remaining on the stem. The classic reflexes are

* /iː/ > /ɪ/ ~ /ɛ/   divine /dɪˈvaɪn/ > divinity /dɪˈvɪnɪti/
* /eɪ/ > /ɛ/ ~ /æ/   please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/
* /aɪ/ > /ɪ/         derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* /iː/ > /ɛ/         serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/
* /eɪ/ > /æ/         grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætıˌtjuːd/

and the same shortening is the reason for the /aɪ/ > /ɪ/ of derive >
derivative, the /iː/ > /ɛ/ of serene > serenity, the /iː/ > /ɛ/ of
please > pleasant and the /eɪ/ > /æ/ of grate > gratitude. All of those
are the normal polysyllabic laxings of the stem vowel under the
addition of -ive, -ity, -ant, -itude etc.

southern < OE sūþern ‘south + -ern’ is /ˈsaʊðən/ ~ /ˈsʌðən/. The stem
south /saʊθ/ keeps its diphthong /aʊ/ in the suffixed form and the form
is only disyllabic, so no trisyllabic shortening of the stem vowel
ever takes place. In the usual textbook sets shadow is also a
disyllabic development, the /eɪ/ > /æ/ of shade > shadow being an
older Old English/Middle English shortening rather than a
product of trisyllabic laxing, which is why southern is the clear
odd-one-out of the six.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: shadow

The set is the classic trisyllabic shortening / laxing set. 
derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvəʔɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
grate /greɪt/ ~ grateful /ˈɡreɪtfl/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtud/  /eɪ/ > /æ/

All four are the familiar long → lax shortening that is regularly associated with the addition of a second unstressed syllable after the stressed vowel, the textbook trisyllabic laxing/ shortening environment. 

shadow < OE sceadu is a native disyllabic root with no suffix-derived long-vowel base. Its stressed vowel /æ/ as in /ˈʃædoʊ/ is the regular reflex of the Old English vowel and it has not been shortened / laxed by a later tri-syllabic environment. Southern is disyllabic in Modern English and is normally cited as a case of vowel reduction rather than classic trisyllabic shortening, which is why shadow is the clear non-member of the laxing set.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the strict phonological sense trisyllabic laxing is a shortening/
laxing of the vowel in a stressed syllable that is followed by two or more
unstressed syllables in a word of three or more syllables.

* derivative < derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* serenity < serene /səˈriːn/ > /səˈrɛnəti/
* gratitude < grate /ɡreɪt/ > /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/

are the classic Modern English cases. The stressed vowel is tense/long in
the disyllabic base and is laxed in the trisyllabic derivative.

southern /ˈsʌðən/, pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ and shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ are all
disyllabic in present-day English, stress + one unstressed syllable, so
they cannot be the site of genuine trisyllabic laxing. Of the three the
clearest non-example is shadow, a Germanic disyllable whose /æ/ is
stable, e.g. shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/. Southern and pleasant are
disyllabic for the same reason and are therefore also not cases of
trisyllabic laxing, the vowel change they show being due to normal
morpho-phonemic reduction / Great Vowel Shift shortening rather than to
the three-syllable environment.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: shadow

Trisyllabic laxing is the English Latinate shortening/laxation that turns a
tense stressed vowel of a base into a lax vowel when the base is extended
with a further unstressed syllable or two. The classic Latinate sets are

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > deriv- /ɪ/ in derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > seren- /ɛ/ in serenity /səˈrɛnəti/
* please /pliːz/ > pleas- /ɛ/ in pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/
* grate /ɡreɪt/ > grat- /æ/ in gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/

and in the same way southern /ˈsʌðən/ shows the Germanic reduction of
south /saʊθ/ > south-ern. 

shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is the Germanic native item < OE sceadu. The stressed
vowel is the inherited Germanic /æ/ and the word is disyllabic with a
tense final diphthong /oʊ/. There is no Latinate base with a tense
/iː, eɪ, aɪ, oʊ/ which is laxed by the addition of a third syllable, i.e.
no trisyllabic laxation has taken place in its history. In that sense
southern and pleasant are also disyllabic, but shadow is the only item in
the set whose vowel quality is not the reflex of a classic Latinate
tense-to-lax shortening at all.

5.text:
Trisyllabic laxing is the shortening/laxing of a tense vowel that is
stressed in a word which is then lengthened by the addition of one or
more unstressed syllables, e.g.

* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛn.ə.ti/
* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/
* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/

and the same type of /iː/ > /ɪ/ ~ /ɛ/ and /aɪ/ > /ɪ/ development that is
normally discussed under the heading of trisyllabic laxing.

The three items that are really disyllabic in Present-Day English,
southern /ˈsʌðən/, pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ and shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/, can
therefore by definition not be cases of trisyllabic laxing.  The
clearest non-cognate of the set is shadow.  Shadow < OE sceadu < PGmc
*skadwō is a native disyllabic word with an historic short *a /æ/; the
/aɪ/ of the simplex shade /ʃeɪd/ is not the source of the /æ/ of
shadow and the form shows no tense > lax development at all, let alone
a development conditioned by an increase to three syllables.

The same point is made in the trisyllabic set.  Derivative and serenity
are the textbook instances of /aɪ/ > /ɪ/ and /iː/ > /ɛ/ laxing under the
addition of unstressed syllables.  Gratitude /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/ is a real
trisyllabic word, but its first-syllable vowel was short in the Latin
source gratitudo < gratus and it never shows the tense-vowel to lax
vowel alternation that defines trisyllabic laxing; it is therefore the
only genuinely trisyllabic item in the list that is not a classic
laxation.  Southern and pleasant/shadow are disyllabic and so are
trivially outside the environment.

8.text:
Trisyllabic laxing / three-syllable shortening is the regular
English shortening/laxing of a tense stressed vowel when the
stressed syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables

* /iː/ → /ɪ/ ~ /ɛ/  ‘divine’ /dɪˈvaɪn/ > ‘divinity’ /dɪˈvɪnəti/
* /eɪ/ → /ɛ/ ~ /æ/  ‘please’ /pliːz/ > ‘pleasant’ /ˈplɛzənt/
* /aɪ/ → /ɪ/      ‘derive’ /dɪˈraɪv/ > ‘derivative’ /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* /iː/ → /ɛ/      ‘serene’ /səˈriːn/ > ‘serenity’ /səˈrɛnəti/

etc. The vowel that is laxed has to be tense in the base form and
the derived form has to be really three-syllable + in the sense of
stressed vowel + two unstressed syllables.

That is the history of

* derivative   di-RAIV > di-RIV-a-tive  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serenity     se-REE-ne > se-REN-i-ty  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* pleasant     PLEEZ > PLEZ-ant         /iː/ > /ɛ/
* gratitude    GRATE-itude  /eɪ/ > /æ/  in the normal trisyllabic
  shortening set

Southern and pleasant and shadow are synchronically disyllabic,
and the cleanest morphological non-example of the set is shadow.
Shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is a Germanic noun-formation with -ow
and the /eɪ/ > /æ/ change is the regular Great-Vowel-Shift / 
assimilatory shortening of *sceadu, not the regular stressed-vowel
laxing that is triggered by the addition of two post-stress
syllables. In the usual textbook list the genuine three-syllable
shortenings are derivative, serenity, pleasant and gratitude; 
shadow, and in the same way the disyllabic southern /ˈsʌðən/
~ /ˈsaʊðən/, is the item that never enters a true trisyllabic
laxing environment.  That is the sense in which southern/pleasant/
shadow are the non-trisyllabic items of the set, with shadow being
the canonical morphological non-example.

derived adjective.  All of them are historically the outcome of a

suffixation.  Hence it has no trisyllabic-laxing history at all; in
the set southern and pleasant are also synchronically disyllabic and

canonical trisyllabic-laxing examples being gratitude, derivative and

Trisyllabic laxing = shortening/laxation of a tense/long stressed vowel when the stressed syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables, normally a Romance/Latinate development. Classic pairs: derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/ /aɪ/>/ɪ/; serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/ /iː/>/ɛ/; please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ /iː/>/ɛ/; grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætıˌtjuːd/ /eɪ/>/æ/.

Derivative and serenity are textbook trisyllabic laxings. Gratitude is usually treated with them, although Colleague 5 notes its first-syllable vowel was already short in Latin gratitudo < gratus and it never shows a tense > lax alternation, so it is a borderline case.

No Latinate base with a tense vowel is laxed by addition of a third syllable; the /eɪ/ > /æ/ relation shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow is an older Germanic/OE shortening, not three-syllable conditioning.

reflection_text.2:
The question is which of southern, derivative, serenity, pleasant, gratitude, shadow has not undergone trisyllabic laxing / three-syllable shortening.

Trisyllabic laxing = shortening/laxation of a tense/long stressed vowel when the stressed syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables, normally a Romance/Latinate development. Classic pairs: derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/ /aɪ/>/ɪ/; serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/ /iː/>/ɛ/; please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ /iː/>/ɛ/; grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætıˌtjuːd/ /eɪ/>/æ/.

Derivative and serenity are textbook trisyllabic laxings. Gratitude is usually treated with them, although Colleague 5 notes its first-syllable vowel was already short in Latin gratitudo < gratus and it never shows a tense > lax alternation, so it is a borderline case.

Pleasant is routinely cited with derivative/serenity/gratitude as a Latinate shortening, even though synchronically it is disyllabic /ˈplɛzənt/. The same is true for southern /ˈsaʊðən/~/ˈsʌðən/ < OE sūþerne. It is disyllabic, stress + one unstressed syllable, and its /aʊ/ is the regular reflex of OE /uː/, not a product of trisyllabic laxing.

Shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ < OE sceadu, PGmc *skadwō is a native Germanic disyllabic word with an inherited short vowel /æ/. No Latinate base with a tense vowel is laxed by addition of a third syllable; the /eɪ/ > /æ/ relation shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow is an older Germanic/OE shortening, not three-syllable conditioning.

Most colleagues 1,4,6,7,9,10 select shadow as the clear non-member. Colleague 2 argues for southern as the odd-one-out, saying shadow is also disyllabic but southern is the canonical Germanic disyllable that never enters a trisyllabic environment, while pleasant is still counted as laxing. Colleague 3 notes southern, pleasant and shadow are all synchronically disyllabic so cannot be sites of genuine trisyllabic laxing, with shadow the clearest non-example.

Unresolved tension: strict phonological definition requires a three-syllable word at the time of change vs the traditional historical set where pleasant and sometimes gratitude are still listed. I currently lean to shadow as the canonical item that never had a long stressed vowel to be laxed in a three-syllable environment; southern is also a non-example by syllable count, and the exact status of pleasant and gratitude remains contested in the discussion.

reflection_text.8:
The question is about vowel shortening/laxation of a tense stressed vowel when the stressed syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables in a Latinate-derived form. * Shadow < OE sceadu < PGmc *skadwō is consistently described as a native Germanic disyllabic root with an historically short *a /æ/.   - grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/

Disagreement / unresolved nuance:
* Gratitude: majority treats it as a trisyllabic shortening example. Colleague 5 notes its first-syllable vowel was short in Latin gratitudo < gratus and therefore there is no tense > lax alternation in the same way as derive/serene; it is trisyllabic but not a classic tense-to-lax case.

Under that strictness pleasant, southern and shadow are all disyllabic and thus trivially outside the environment. Current leaning: shadow is the consensus pick for “has not undergone trisyllabic laxing”; it is the only item with no Latinate tense-vowel base and no history of long-to-lax conditioning. Southern is the other disyllabic Germanic oddity and is the alternative pick in a strictly syllable-count sense. Pleasant is contested between textbook inclusion and strict syllable-count exclusion. Gratitude is mostly accepted as a textbook example, with a minority caveat about its Latin short vowel origin.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Shadow remains the clearest non-example. The process requires a historically tense vowel in a base that then laxes under addition of two further unstressed syllables, exactly as in derive–derivative, serene–serenity, please–pleasant and grate–gratitude. Shadow descends directly from the Old English disyllable sceadu with an inherited short *a; it never possessed a long-vowel simplex whose quality was altered by a trisyllabic environment. Southern shows the same native disyllabic profile, but its /aʊ/ ~ /ʌ/ alternation is a later reduction rather than the canonical Romance-style laxing. The other four items all display the textbook tense-to-lax shift conditioned by suffixation that produced three or more syllables, so shadow is the item that has simply never undergone the change.

The disyllabic surface forms of pleasant and southern do not disqualify them; the historical conditioning still applies.

Shadow is the canonical non-member of the set.

Trisyllabic laxing / three-syllable shortening is the shortening/laxation of a tense/long stressed vowel when the stressed syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables in a learned/Latinate derivative, e.g.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/

Derivative and serenity are textbook cases. Pleasant and gratitude are routinely cited with them as the same type of Romance/Latinate stem vowel shortening, even if synchronically pleasant is disyllabic /ˈplɛzənt/.

Shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ < OE sceadu, PGmc *skadwō is an inherited native Germanic disyllabic root. Its stressed /æ/ is the regular reflex of OE a/æ and it has never had a tense long stressed vowel that is laxed by the addition of a third syllable. The /eɪ/ > /æ/ relation shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow is an older Germanic/OE shortening, not three-syllable conditioning.

Southern /ˈsaʊðən/~/ˈsʌðən/ < OE sūþerne is also synchronically disyllabic and Germanic, and by strict syllable count it likewise cannot be a site of genuine trisyllabic laxing. That is the tension in the list: southern, pleasant and shadow are all disyllabic today. Of those, shadow is the clearest morphological non-example because it is a native Germanic disyllable with an historically short vowel and no Latinate base with a tense vowel to be laxed at all, whereas pleasant is still traditionally classed with the Latinate shortening set.

4.text:
Shadow is the canonical non-member.

Trisyllabic laxing/shortening is the Modern English Latinate development in which a tense/long stressed vowel of a simplex base is shortened/laxed when the stem is extended to a stressed + two unstressed syllable environment, e.g.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/

Derivative and serenity are the textbook three-syllable cases. Pleasant and gratitude are routinely cited with them as the same Latinate tense > lax shortening, pleasant even though it is synchronically disyllabic, and gratitude even though the first syllable vowel was already short in Latin *gratus/gratitudo*.

Southern /ˈsaʊðən/ ~ /ˈsʌðən/ < OE sūðerne is a Germanic disyllabic adjective. There is never a stressed + two unstressed syllable stage and the /aʊ/ ~ /ʌ/ alternation is regular Germanic vowel reduction, not Latinate trisyllabic laxing.

Shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ < OE sceadu, PGmc *skadwō is even clearer. It is a native Germanic disyllabic root with an inherited short *a > /æ/. There is no Latinate simplex with a tense /iː eɪ aɪ/ base from which /æ/ could be derived by trisyllabic conditioning, and shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is Old English/Middle English shortening/ Great Vowel Shift development, not a stressed-vowel laxation triggered by the addition of a third syllable. It therefore has no trisyllabic-laxing history at all, whereas the other four items do show the classic Latinate tense-to-lax shortening. Southern and pleasant are also synchronically disyllabic, but shadow is the morphological non-example par excellence.

Pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ < please /pliːz/ /iː/ > /ɛ/ and gratitude /ˈɡrætıˌtjuːd/ < grate /ɡreɪt/ /eɪ/ > /æ/ are routinely cited in the same Latinate shortening set, the vowel being laxed on the addition of -ant/-itude. The Latin source of gratitude is short in the source, but synchronically it is the normal /eɪ/ ~ /æ/ trisyllabic pair.

Trisyllabic laxing is the Modern English Latinate shortening/laxation of a tense stressed vowel when the stem is extended so that the stressed syllable is followed by two unstressed syllables, i.e. stressed + unstressed + unstressed.

On that strict environment

* derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/ < derive /dɪˈraɪv/ : /aɪ/ > /ɪ/  in the -ative trisyllabic derivative.
* serenity /səˈrɛnəti/ < serene /səˈriːn/ : /iː/ > /ɛ/  in the -ity trisyllabic derivative.

are textbook.

gratitude /ˈɡræ.tɪ.tuːd/ is the usual textbook illustration of /eɪ/ > /æ/  grate > gratitude, and pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ < please /pliːz/ is routinely cited with that set as the Romance /iː/ > /ɛ/ shortening.  Synchronically pleasant and southern are disyllabic, stress + one unstressed syllable, so they are not the classic antepenultimate-stress trisyllabic environment, and pleasant’s reduction is more properly disyllabic shortening/Great Vowel Shift reduction. Gratitude is also controversial on etymological grounds, the Latin source gratitudo < gratus already having a short vowel, so it is not a pure tense > lax alternation in English.

shadow is different in kind.  /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ < OE sceadu < PGmc *skadwō is an inherited Germanic disyllabic root with an original short *a /æ/.  There is no Latinate tense base /eɪ, iː, aɪ/ which is laxed by the addition of a third syllable, and the /eɪ/ of shade /ʃeɪd/ is not the direct simplex source of the /æ/ of shadow. The vowel quality is the regular reflex of Old English a before /d/ and the formation is a native Germanic noun formation with -ow. No three-syllable conditioning ever applies to it.

Southern /ˈsʌðən/ ~ /ˈsaʊðən/ < OE sūðerne is on the same footing as far as the strict stressed + two unstressed syllables condition is concerned: it is synchronically disyllabic and the diphthong /aʊ/ is the regular reflex of OE /uː/, not the product of trisyllabic laxing.

Of the six items shadow is the canonical morphological non-member: it has no trisyllabic laxation history at all. Southern is the other disyllabic Germanic odd man out; pleasant and gratitude are the usual, if debated, Latinate shortening cases.

6.text:
Trisyllabic laxing / three-syllable shortening is the Latinate Modern English 
shortening/laxation of a tense stressed vowel in a disyllabic base when the
stem is extended to a stressed vowel + two or more unstressed syllables,
and in the textbook Romance set the base vowel is tense/long and the
derived vowel is lax/short.

That is the history of the Latinate items in the list

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvəti v/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/, routinely cited with the
  above set
* grate- > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtud/  /eɪ/ > /æ/ in the -itude environment

All four show the classic tense → lax alternation under the addition of a
learned suffix. Pleasant is synchronically disyllabic /ˈplɛzənt/, and southern
/ˈsaʊðən/ ~ /ˈsʌðən/ is also synchronically disyllabic, so in the strict
stressed+two-unstressed sense they are marginal, but they are still treated
in the literature as the Latinate shortening type.

Shadow is different in kind. /ˈʃædoʊ/ < OE sceadu < PGmc *skadwō is an
inherited Germanic disyllable with an original short *a /æ/. There is no
Latinate base with a tense /iː, eɪ, aɪ, oʊ/ that is laxed by the addition of a
third syllable. The /eɪ/ > /æ/ relation shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is an
Old English / Middle English Germanic noun formation with -ow and a
regular Germanic vowel development, not a tense-to-lax shortening
conditioned by a trisyllabic stress environment.

Hence on the usual textbook classification shadow is the clear morphological
non-member of the trisyllabic laxing set. Southern is the other Germanic
disyllabic item in the list and is also outside the canonical Latinate
tense-to-lax environment; the canonical trisyllabic-laxing examples in the
six-item set are derivative, serenity, gratitude and, in the conventional
treatment, pleasant, with shadow as the canonical native Germanic
non-example.

* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/

There is never a tense long-vowel base that is laxed by extension to a three-syllable stressed form, and the word has no Latinate trisyllabic conditioning in its history.
